paras: The killing of Raymond Sizer was the fatal shooting of Sizer, a young Black man, by seventeen-year-old Clarence M. Brooks, a white storekeeper's son, in the Brooks store at Vaughanville, Newberry County, South Carolina, on October 10, 1903. By the Brooks family's sworn account the quarrel began when Brooks demanded to be called "Mr. Brooks"; a coroner's jury found self-defense, and a jury acquitted him of murder on November 5. A week later about fifty armed white men gathered at Vaughanville and the Black Odd Fellows' hall burned, which the Newberry Herald and News said made the case "well-known throughout the State."

C. A. Brooks kept a store on his land near his house in upper Newberry County, and his sons Clarence, 17, and Walter, 15, slept in it at night. The Herald and News described Sizer as a prominent member of the Black Odd Fellows' lodge, which it said had "long been a disturbing element in the community."

At about 10:30 that Saturday night Sizer knocked and called on Clarence to open the door; both brothers testified that Clarence replied his name was "Mr. Brooks, to a negro." After Walter sold Sizer goods, they said, Sizer cursed and refused to call Clarence "Mister," and Clarence ordered him out. Clarence testified that when cursed again he struck Sizer in the face with a pistol, while Walter said Sizer struck first; both said Sizer then came at Clarence with an iron weight and Clarence shot him through the heart.

An inquest the next day before Magistrate J. W. Ropp heard only the three Brooks family members and found that Brooks acted "in self defense—or to protect his life." Sizer's mother and stepfather refused the body, on instructions from leaders of a nearby Black meeting according to the paper, so white men including the magistrate and Brooks's attorney, Cole L. Blease, buried it in the woods. The next day Black residents exhumed the body and reburied it about a mile away.

On Friday, October 16, a report spread that Black residents had sent for arms and would meet at the Odd Fellows' hall before calling on Brooks and on the men who had buried Sizer. About thirty-five white men "armed to the teeth" gathered at Whit Goodwyn's store and were joined by twelve from Newberry. A detachment found the hall dark and empty, and soon afterward the building, which also housed a Black school, burned to the ground; how the fire started was not known. A proposal to visit five named Black "ringleaders" and "give them correction" was voted down after Blease, Fred H. Dominick, Deputy Sheriff Duncan Johnson and Constable C. G. Blease opposed it.

Brooks, free on $200 bond, was tried for murder at the Newberry court of general sessions with Blease as counsel. On November 5, after "very little testimony," he was "promptly acquitted." No report of an inquiry into the hall fire appears in the coverage.

All the coverage found is from white papers, chiefly the Newberry Herald and News, which printed the inquest testimony under the headline "JUSTIFIABLE HOMICIDE" and called the shooter "Mr. Clarence Brooks." Its October 20 report on the expected "race trouble" presented the armed gathering as protective, called the Newberry party "AN ORDERLY CROWD," blamed the Odd Fellows' "baneful influence," and dismissed a rumor that a Black man had been shot dead near the hall. It warned that had Black residents made any demonstration "blood would have been freely spilt."

Outside Newberry, the Lancaster Ledger ran a short dispatch, "WHITE MAN KILLS A NEGRO," saying Sizer "cursed and gave Mr. Brooks some impudence" before raising a weight, with no mention of the demand to be called "Mr." or the pistol blow.

The brothers disagreed on who struck first, Clarence saying he hit Sizer with his pistol after being cursed and Walter saying Sizer struck first. Every version comes from the Brooks family, the only witnesses sworn, and no account from Sizer's side appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Killing of Raymond Sizer
bases: A single white youth shot a Black man in his father's store after a quarrel over addressing him as 'Mr.' (A1, A4); the armed white gathering and burning of the Black Odd Fellows' hall a week later (A5, A6) is a related community episode.

The local Herald and News inquest report (A1) and a separate Newberry dispatch in the Lancaster Ledger (A4) agree that Brooks shot and killed Sizer at the store, and later court reports confirm the murder charge and acquittal (A9, A10); every account of how the shooting happened traces to the Brooks family.

accounts.label: Clarence M. Brooks (inquest testimony)
accounts.gist: Sizer refused to call him 'Mr. Brooks' and cursed him; Clarence ordered him out and, when cursed again, struck him with a pistol; Sizer came at him with a weight and he shot him, fearing for his life.

accounts.label: Walter C. Brooks (inquest testimony)
accounts.gist: Same dispute over 'Mister'; says Sizer struck Clarence first, then Clarence hit him with the pistol, Sizer picked up a weight, and Clarence shot him.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Sizer died of a gunshot wound inflicted by Clarence M. Brooks 'acting in self defense'.

accounts.label: Newberry dispatch
accounts.gist: Sizer cursed and gave 'impudence' while leaving, refused to go when told, and picked up a weight to strike Brooks, who shot him.

accounts.label: Vaughanville whites (via Herald and News)
accounts.gist: The Black Odd Fellows held frequent meetings and made threats after Sizer's death and planned to call on Brooks; the armed white gathering was to protect the community.

framing.detail: The Newberry Herald and News headlined the inquest 'JUSTIFIABLE HOMICIDE', called the shooter 'Mr. Clarence Brooks', blamed the Black Odd Fellows' 'baneful influence', and called it 'a matter of congratulation' that the armed night ended quietly.
The Lancaster Ledger ran a short Newberry dispatch, 'WHITE MAN KILLS A NEGRO', giving the Brooks version that Sizer gave 'impudence' and raised a weight.

versions.value: Clarence struck Sizer with a pistol after being cursed, before Sizer took up the weight (Clarence's testimony)
Sizer struck Clarence first, then Clarence hit him with the pistol (Walter's testimony)
No pistol blow mentioned: Sizer cursed or insulted Brooks and came at him with a weight

conflicts.note: All versions come from the Brooks family; Clarence's own testimony is the only one in which he admits striking first. No account from Sizer's side was found.
Minor; both place Vaughanville in the upper part of the county.

white press only: Newberry Herald and News (Oct. 13, Oct. 20, Nov. 3, Nov. 6) and Lancaster Ledger (Oct. 14); no Black-press coverage found
